MFQ purity items are rated about as morally relevant as its loyalty and authority items, which the authors concede contradicts the theory. The data cannot be shared. | Read |
| [NOTE-428](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-428.md) | How effective psychological treatments work: mechanisms of change in cognitive behavioural therapy and beyond | A history-and-argument paper. It separates common factors from mechanisms of change, holds that a treatment's success does not validate its theory, and proposes one mechanism for all effective therapy: the person, "stuck" in an exaggerated negative meaning (Theory A) maintained by their own reactions, builds and tests a less threatening alternative (Theory B), a meaning-making flexibility. The proposal is argued from clinical examples and cited trials. The paper itself says mechanism research has not yet met Kazdin's standards. | Read |
| [NOTE-429](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-429.md) | The Emerging Field of Emotion Regulation: An Integrative Review | Gross's founding review. Emotions are modulable response tendencies. Regulation, defined as influencing which emotions one has, when, and how they are experienced and expressed, is split from coping, mood regulation and defense, and sorted into five families by where it acts in emotion generation: situation selection, situation modification, attentional deployment, cognitive change, response modulation. The paper's own open problem is whether regulation can be told apart from generation at all. | Read |
| [NOTE-430](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-430.md) | Relational Frame Theory: Some Implications for Understanding and Treating Human Psychopathology | RFT stated for clinicians. Human relating is bidirectional and arbitrarily applicable, a generalized operant under contextual control, with mutual and combinatorial entailment and transformation of function. Relating relations explains metaphor, rules are networks whose coordination with events regulates behaviour, and the self is content, process and context. These are offered as the reason direct-contingency behaviour therapy is "inadequate", and ACT's acceptance, defusion and values are given RFT readings explicitly labelled heuristic. | Read |
| [NOTE-431](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-431.md) | Acceptance and Commitment Therapy: Model, Processes and Outcomes | The ACT model, read in an early manuscript. Psychopathology is psychological inflexibility: cognitive fusion (fed by literality, reason-giving and emotional control) supports experiential avoidance, and both displace present-moment contact and values. Six processes restore flexibility. The manuscript's evidence: AAQ correlations with distress (21 studies), component studies of acceptance and defusion, mediation in seven trials, and weighted outcome effect sizes (d = .49 post and .69 follow-up against active treatments). | Read |
| [NOTE-436](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-436.md) | Psychological Flexibility as a Fundamental Aspect of Health | A narrative review that defines psychological flexibility by four dynamic abilities (adapting to situations, reconfiguring resources, shifting perspective, balancing domains). Flexible regulation beats any fixed strategy (Bonanno 2004; Cheng 2001). Inflexibility marks depression and anxiety, and cardiac vagal control may integrate its forms. Causal direction is open. It recommends experience sampling and multi-informant measures over global self-report. | Read |
| [NOTE-437](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-437.md) | The Future of Intervention Science: Process-Based Therapy | A programme paper. Thirty years of DSM-linked trials never turned syndromes into diseases, so evidence-based therapy should target theory-derived, empirically supported processes of change with procedures shown to move them. Its distinctive commitments are a falsification rule for models of change, moderated mediation as a basis for a new nosology, and an idiographic, functional-analytic diagnosis. It offers predictions and cited examples, not new data. | Read |
| [NOTE-438](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-438.md) v2 | A meta-analytic review of experiments examining the effects of extrinsic rewards on intrinsic motivation | 128 experiments on interesting tasks, separate meta-analyses for free-choice behaviour and self-reported interest. Tangible rewards expected for engaging in, completing or doing well at a task undermine free-choice intrinsic motivation (d from −0.28 to −0.40), and less so self-reports; unexpected and task-noncontingent rewards do not; positive feedback enhances, except for children's free choice. The pattern fits cognitive evaluation theory and contradicts Eisenberger and Cameron's helplessness and learned-industriousness account. | Read |
| [NOTE-439](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-439.md) | The "What" and "Why" of Goal Pursuits: Human Needs and the Self-Determination of Behavior | Needs in SDT are innate psychological nutriments, identified functionally by the costs of their thwarting, not by individual differences in their strength. The three needs organize findings on intrinsic motivation and internalization, predict that both the "why" (autonomous vs controlled regulation) and the "what" (intrinsic vs extrinsic aspirations) of goals affect well-being, and explain need substitutes and rigid defences when needs are thwarted. Autonomy is self-organization, defended as an evolved, domain-general design feature. | Read |
| [NOTE-440](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-440.md) | Basic psychological need theory: Advancements, critical themes, and future directions | The authors set out nine criteria a basic psychological need must meet, separate need frustration from mere lack of satisfaction, review need frustration's costs (ill-being, compensatory behaviour, need substitutes) and propose it as transdiagnostic, review the interplay with sleep, food, sex and safety, map need-supportive and need-thwarting practices on a circumplex, and argue that the needs are universal in their effects ("output side") while the practices that satisfy them vary ("input side"). Novelty, morality and beneficence are weighed as fourth needs and not yet admitted. | Read |
| [NOTE-441](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-441.md) | Self-Regulation and the Problem of Human Autonomy: Does Psychology Need Choice, Self-Determination, and Will? | SDT's autonomy is "regulation by the self": acting with reflective endorsement, graded along the internalization continuum, compatible with external influence, dependence and a single option. Ryan and Deci align it with phenomenological and hierarchical (Frankfurt, Dworkin) accounts and use that definition to answer behaviourist, social-cognitive, reductionist, nonconscious-priming, choice-overload and cultural critiques. Autonomy lies not in being an uncaused cause but in the capacity to "reflectively endorse or reject prompted actions" (p. 1573). | Read |
| [NOTE-442](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-442.md) v2 | Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being | SDT's canonical short statement. Social contexts that support competence, autonomy and relatedness sustain intrinsic motivation and let people internalize and integrate extrinsic regulations; controlling, rejecting or overchallenging contexts undermine intrinsic motivation and leave regulations external or introjected. Autonomy is graded: four kinds of extrinsic motivation lie on a continuum of relative autonomy (Ryan & Connell's quasi-simplex). Basic needs are defined by their consequences for well-being, and need-deprivation is offered as a principal source of distress and psychopathology. | Read |
| [NOTE-443](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-443.md) | Précis of Breakdown of Will | Hyperbolic discounting makes preference reverse with delay alone, so a person is a population of interests that forestall one another. Will is the recursive bundling of choices by treating each as a precedent, which gives an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma and makes Kavka's toxin rational to drink. The same recursion predicts legalism, "lapse districts", motivated misperception and compulsive over-control, and premature satiation of appetite limits what will can do for emotional reward. | Read |
| [NOTE-448](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-448.md) | Goal Striving, Need Satisfaction, and Longitudinal Well-Being: The Self-Concordance Model | Sheldon and Elliot's integrated model of goal striving. Self-concordance (identified + intrinsic − introjected − external reasons) predicts sustained effort, effort fully mediates attainment (Study 1 β = .02 ns vs .76; Study 3 β = .08 ns vs .72), attainment predicts change in well-being more strongly when goals are self-concordant (interaction β = .11, .23), and accumulated daily autonomy, competence and relatedness partly mediate attainment's effect on well-being (Study 3). Three correlational student samples; SEM fits reached after adding paths the modification indices suggested. | Read |
| [NOTE-452](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-452.md) | The Intimate Contest for Self-Command | Schelling's essay proposes "egonomics", the art of managing oneself. Its core claim is that many self-control tactics are the tactics for managing another person, applied to a "sometime self" who will be in command later. It gives a taxonomy of habits by time profile, onset time, warning time, cost, visibility, damage function and self-aggravation. It refuses a general answer to which self is authentic. It estimates the stakes at "on the order of a trillion dollars" for the current population. | Read |
| [NOTE-469](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-469.md) | Thine Own Self: True Self-Concept Accessibility and Meaning in Life | Five studies with students. True-self accessibility, the residual speed of "me" judgments for one's own true-self traits, predicts MLQ presence of meaning (β = .29, .24, .19 in Studies 1, 2, 4) beyond actual-self accessibility, affect, need satisfaction, liking, overlap, state self-esteem and AI-3 authenticity. Subliminal true-self primes raised reported meaning against actual-self primes (Study 3, ANCOVA F = 4.46) and against disliked actual-self primes (Study 5, contrast F = 5.07), with disliked true-self traits as effective as liked ones. | Read |
| [NOTE-470](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-470.md) | “First we invented stories, then they changed us”: The Evolution of Narrative Identity | McAdams's review essay on narrative identity: "the internalized and evolving story a person invents to explain how he or she has become the person he or she is becoming". Storytelling is placed in human evolution as a tool for simulating social life and binding groups. The self is layered as actor, then agent, then author, with the life story arriving in adolescence on the back of autobiographical memory, theory of mind and autobiographical reasoning. Story features predict well-being and generativity. Culture supplies master narratives. Claims are cited, not shown. | Read |
| [NOTE-550](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-550.md) | List & Pettit — Group Agency and Supervenience | Four conditions of agency (§2). A group's judgments supervene on members' contributions under a constitution (§3). With a universal domain, robust group rationality is inconsistent with majoritarian, uniform proposition-wise and proposition-wise supervenience (Propositions 1–3), and consistent with set-wise supervenience, as the premise-based and distributed premise-based procedures show (Propositions 4–5; Table 4). The group's judgment on a conclusion can be fixed by members' judgments on premises alone. Emergent agency without members' conception of the group is judged unintelligible (§6). | Read |
| [NOTE-551](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-551.md) | The Ripple Effect: Emotional Contagion and its Influence on Group Behavior | Study 1 (94 undergraduates, 29 groups, 2×2 confederate valence × energy): members' mood followed the confederate's valence (self-report change +.41 vs −.26, χ²(1) = 9.97; coders 2.75 vs 2.33, χ²(1) = 10.30). Pleasant contagion predicted self- and peer-rated cooperativeness, coder-rated group cooperativeness (r = .44) and lower conflict (r = −.42 to −.48). Valence asymmetry failed (χ² < 1) and energy effects were marginal and opposite in sign. Study 2 (113 MBA students, 26 groups, no confederate): mood ICC rose from .00 to .24; contagion correlated with cooperation (.49) and conflict (−.49). | Read |
| [NOTE-552](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-552.md) | Towards a Theory of Collective Emotions | Collective emotion as synchronous convergence in affective responding towards one event or object. The minimal case needs only shared appraisal structures. Mutual awareness (contagion, mediated sharing) and group membership (identity, collective intentions, norms, collective memory, group-based sentiments) amplify it and change its quality, including a transition from "I-mode" to "We-mode" collective emotion. A conceptual synthesis with no data; the authors say the key linkages lack evidence. | Read |
| [NOTE-554](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-554.md) | List — Three kinds of collective attitudes | Aggregate attitudes: a rule or market summarises members' attitudes; proposition-wise supervenience; no direct role; rationality contingent (majority beliefs on p, q, p∧q can be inconsistent, Table 1). Common attitudes: all hold, with common awareness; enriched proposition-wise supervenience; coordination; consistent by unanimity. Corporate attitudes: a group agent's; holistic supervenience, like non-reductive physicalism; action-guiding; rationality presupposed. Three lessons of near-independence; Table 2 summarises. | Read |
| [NOTE-561](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-561.md) | Double-Loop Learning, Teaching, and Research | Defines single- and double-loop learning and restates the theory of action. People espouse many theories but act on one, Model I, which keeps reasoning tacit and makes errors in governing values undiscussable. That produces self-sealing individual and organizational defensive routines. A CEO workshop transcript shows the pattern, and a quasi-experimental design to test it is proposed but not run. | Read |
| [NOTE-563](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-563.md) | Beyond Markets and States: Polycentric Governance of Complex Economic Systems | Ostrom's retrospective. Polycentric arrangements, many formally independent decision centres, can outperform single hierarchies. Long-surviving common-pool resource institutions share eight design principles, not specific rules. In experiments communication and self-chosen sanctions sustain cooperation, and in the field local monitoring predicts outcomes. No single regime type is a panacea. | Read |
| [NOTE-566](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-566.md) | "Exit, Voice, and Loyalty": Further Reflections and a Survey of Recent Contributions | Hirschman revisits Exit, Voice, and Loyalty. Voice deserves more weight than he gave it: it can be felt as a benefit, it carries richer information than exit, and it suits goods whose quality nobody fully knows. Exit can be costly without loyalty and can convey nothing. An organization needs floor levels of both for feedback and cannot survive beyond ceilings; managers may favour the response least threatening to them. | Read |
| [NOTE-577](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-577.md) | The Viable System Model: Its Provenance, Development, Methodology and Pathology | Beer's retrospective on the Viable System Model. Five subsystems are necessary and sufficient for any organism or organization to keep its identity independently, and the structure recurs at every level. The model is defended as a scientific model built by homomorphic mapping, testable but never proved. Pathologies are traced to failing subsystems, chiefly the collapse of Three and Five when Four is missing. Evidence is the author's recollected consultancy. | Read |
| [NOTE-578](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-578.md) | History As Cause: Columbia and Challenger | The Board finds that Columbia and Challenger had the same organizational cause. Evidence that foam shedding and O-ring erosion departed from the design was repeatedly reinterpreted as acceptable, each decision seeming correct in itself. Political and budget constraints, schedule pressure, consensus sign-off, a hierarchy that silenced dissent, and a safety organization dependent on the program sustained the pattern for twenty years and undid post-Challenger reforms. | Read |
| [NOTE-581](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-581.md) | Exploration and Exploitation in Organizational Learning | Exploitation's returns are surer, nearer and closer to the decision than exploration's, so adaptive processes favour it and become self-destructive. In a simulation of mutual learning, an organizational code improves only from members who deviate from it. Slow socialization, a mix of fast and slow learners, and moderate turnover raise what the organization knows; under environmental change without turnover, its knowledge decays to chance. Where only first place counts, variance beats reliability. | Read |
| [NOTE-584](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-584.md) | Risk management in a dynamic society: a modelling problem | Risk management is a control problem across a sociotechnical hierarchy. Under cost and effort gradients, activity migrates toward the boundary of acceptable performance, and redundant defences erode unobserved because breaching one shows no effect. Accidents come from the interaction of many locally reasonable decisions. The remedy is making boundaries visible, not suppressing errors. | Read |
| [NOTE-587](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-587.md) | Pervasive negative effects of rewards on intrinsic motivation: The myth continues | The authors of the 1994 rival meta-analysis re-analyse 145 studies. They accept several of Deci, Koestner and Ryan's corrections, and code reward contingencies by what participants were told rather than by cognitive evaluation theory's categories. Result: no overall effect on free choice; enhancement on low-interest tasks; on high-interest tasks, undermining only for expected tangible rewards loosely tied to performance, or earned at less than the maximum; neutral or positive effects for rewards tied to a standard or to beating others. All of it is small. | Read |
| [NOTE-590](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-590.md) | The stance triangle | Stance is one act with three aspects: in taking a stance a speaker evaluates an object, thereby positions a subject (usually the self), and thereby aligns with other subjects. The triangle's nodes are two subjects and a shared object; its sides are directed vectors of evaluation (two) and alignment, with positioning reflected back on each subject. Stance belongs to utterances in dialogic context, not to sentences, and needs an object even when none is spoken. A stance follow that resonates with a stance lead must mark the relation (too, either). Argued from Santa Barbara Corpus excerpts; no counts are reported. | Read |
| [NOTE-596](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-596.md) | Cumulative cultural evolution in the laboratory | Four chains of ten adults each learned a 27-item artificial language from 14 items and passed their test output on. Transmission error fell and string–meaning structure rose. Unfiltered (Experiment 1), the languages collapsed to 2–5 words that systematically underspecified meanings (colour lost in every chain). With homonyms filtered from training (Experiment 2), they became compositional, with substrings for colour, shape and motion. Participants believed they were copying. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-604](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-604.md) | Wang, Solloway, Shiffrin & Busemeyer, the QQ equality in 72 surveys | Across all 66 Pew surveys of 2001–2011 that varied the order of two questions, chosen without regard to their outcome, question order changes the answers (p = 0.0004 for the order-effect χ² distribution) while the probability of answering the two questions alike does not change (p = 0.4625 for the q values), as the QQ equality predicts. Paired context effects across 72 studies lie along the predicted line of slope −1 (r = −0.82). | Read |
| [NOTE-609](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-609.md) | Computational challenges to Lévi-Strauss transformational methodology | Proposes DEVS modelling and simulation, in the authors' DEVSimPy, as a way to generate and visualise Lévi-Strauss's transformations of myth, and extends the canonical formula's "boundary condition" to a programme on identity politics. What it shows is software: myths as mytheme lists, variants produced by user-specified operations, and one Corsican folktale's mythemes placed on Google Earth. No claim about myth is tested. | Read |
| [NOTE-615](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-615.md) | Морфология сказки | Finds that in a hundred Russian wondertales the stable units are characters' functions, defined by their consequence for the action: 31 of them, in one order, over seven spheres of action, so every wondertale is a selection from one sequence and the variety lies in omissions, realisations and the casting of characters. Plot and variant cannot be separated, tales can be generated from the scheme, and the wondertale is conjectured to be morphologically a myth. | Read |
| [NOTE-618](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-618.md) | Structuralism | From a one-page-in-four preview of chs. I–IV: a structure is defined by wholeness, transformation and self-regulation. Its elements are subordinated to laws of composition; "all known structures… are, without exception, systems of transformation"; and in logic and mathematics regulation is perfect because every operation has an inverse. Structures whose transformations unfold in time, linguistic or social, are regulated but not fully reversible. Structures are real only if governed from within, by a subject defined as "the center of functional activity". | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-628](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-628.md) | Larger communities create more systematic languages | Varies community size alone in a laboratory language-creation game: groups of eight built more systematic, compositional languages than groups of four, faster and more uniformly across groups, while reaching the same communicative success and convergence. Input variability, greater in larger groups, predicted gains in structure; small groups differed more from each other on every measure. | Read |
| [NOTE-632](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-632.md) | Discrete-event simulation of Lévi-Strauss's myth analysis | Specifies the DEVS models behind the authors' Lévi-Strauss simulation. A myth is a list of (term, function) mythemes; homology, inversion, opposition and symmetry are each the replacement of one term by a user-supplied other in every mytheme; mythemes can be added or removed; the canonical formula is described but not given a computation. Reproducing 70 Mythologiques myths and 28 Corsican tales by transformations chosen to produce them is offered as validation of Lévi-Strauss's method; it shows only that the encoding can express them. | Read |
| [NOTE-636](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-636.md) | Wang & Busemeyer, the QQ model and QQ equality | Derives the QQ equality from a Lüders-projection model of answering attitude questions: the probability of answering two questions differently is the same in both orders, for any belief state, any projectors and any dimension, provided only the first answer changes the state before the second. It holds in five of six data sets and fails, as the authors predicted, in the sixth, where new information came between the questions. The argument that classical models fail it is informal. | Read |
| [NOTE-641](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-641.md) | Transformation transformed | Separates structuralism's method from Lévi-Strauss's doctrine and makes transformation its core: a structure is the set of invariant relations that orders passage between variants. Lévi-Strauss transformed in two regimes, Goethean development of an initial form (kinship) and Thompsonian deformation between given forms (myth, where the analyst cuts the continuum); Descola's four ontologies are a Goethean group, and structural comparison the fairest symmetrization anthropology has. | Read |
| [NOTE-642](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-642.md) | Morphology of the Folktale | In chs. II–III of the 1968 English text, Propp's four theses and his 31 functions appear as in the Russian. The functions are named by nouns of action under capitalised headings, with Greek signs for the seven preparatory functions and Latin ones after. "Dramatis personae" and "characters" alternate for the same word, and the class studied is "fairy tales", under a title Dundes calls misleading. The second edition's additions are visible on the page: Wagner's notes correct about forty of Propp's tale references in two chapters and renumber the tales to the later Afanas'ev numbering. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-649](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-649.md) | Large AI models are cultural and social technologies | Argues that large models are a cultural and social technology, not intelligent agents: lossy, uninvertible summaries of human-produced corpora that, like prices and bureaucratic categories, allow the information to be reorganized at scale. The argument is by analogy and classification; no evidence is offered that could have come out otherwise. It names one mechanism (fitting the training distribution on average makes models worst where data are rare, which may homogenize culture) and leaves both it and its remedy untested. | Read |
